Training Deep Neural Network for Optimal Power
Allocation in Islanded Microgrid Systems:
A Distributed Learning-Based Approach
Fanghong Guo , Member , IEEE,B o w e nX u , Wen-An Zhang , Member , IEEE,
Changyun Wen , Fellow, IEEE, Dan Zhang , Senior Member , IEEE,
and Li Y u , Senior Member , IEEE
Abstract— Currently, numerical optimization methods are used
to solve distributed optimal power allocation (OPA) problems for
islanded microgrid (MG) systems. Most of them are developed
based on rigorous mathematical derivation. However, the com-
plexity of such optimization algorithms inevitably creates a
gap between theoretical analysis and real-time implementation.
In order to bridge such a gap, in this article we provide a
new distributed learning-based framework to solve the real-time
OPA problem. Speciﬁcally, inspired by the human-thinking
scheme, distributed deep neural networks (DNNs) together with a
dynamic average consensus algorithm are ﬁrst employed to obtain
an approximate OPA solution in a distributed manner. Then a
distributed balance generation and demand algorithm is designed
to ﬁne-tune it to obtain the ﬁnal optimal feasible solution.
In addition, it is theoretically proved that the proposed DNN can
well approximate one existing OPA algorithm (Guo et al. 2018),
where quantitative numbers of at most how many hidden layers
and neurons are provided. Several experimental case studies show
that our proposed distributed learning framework can achieve
similar optimal results to those obtained by using typical existing
distributed numerical optimization methods while it is superior
in terms of simplicity and real-time capability.
Index Terms— Bio-inspired optimization, deep neural network
(DNN), distributed framework, learning to optimize, optimal
power allocation (OPA).
I. I NTRODUCTION
I

and power consumption need from remote rural areas
and island residents, the c oncept of microgrid (MG) was

According to its deﬁnition, an MG is a small-scale low-voltage
power system that integrates power generation, transmis-
sion, distribution, and consumption together. Different from
fossil-fueled thermal power generators in traditional power
systems, most distributed energy resources (DERs) in MG
system are powered by renewable energy resources such as
photovoltaic and wind turbines. These DERs usually gen-
erate intermittent power, and they are also relatively small
in terms of their power generation capability. Hence more
advanced control and optimization techniques are needed for
the energy management of MG system [3]–[5]. In [6]–[8],
model predictive control (MPC) approaches are utilized in the
energy management for MGs. Its main function is to provide
real-time control of MG together with tracking optimal gen-
eration scheduling r eferences calculated b y some optimization
algorithms. However, how to achieve real-time optimization
to keep up with the pace of real-time control is still a very
challenging topic.
For decades, distributed num erical optimization methods
solving optimal power allocation (OP A) have been attract-
ing a great deal of attention. The work in [9] proposes an
alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) based
distributed optimization algorithm. Li et al. [10] present a
distributed interior point method using a θ-logarithmic barrier.
In [11], a consensus-based distributed regularized primal-dual
subgradient algorithm is developed to avoid projecting the
estimates onto the global constraint set at every iteration
but sacriﬁces a certain so lution accuracy. Wang et al. [12]
propose a distributed extremum-seeking algorithm based on
average analysis. In [1], a hie rarchical decentralized opti-
mization architecture is proposed to solve the OP A, which
requires gradient-based local optimization and an extra coor-
dinator agent to conduct the gl obal operation. In general,
almost all distributed algorith ms focus on the accuracy of the
solution while ignoring the real-time requirements of today’s
distributed systems. In fact, they are suffering from high
computational and communication costs. For example, the case
studies in [10] show that it takes more than 10 s to solve a
single distributed OP A problem on a 3-unit system. The reason
behind this is that these distributed algorithms are almost all

gradient-based, which indicates that at least tens to thousands
of iterations are required while each iteration contains at
least one consensus operation. What’s worse, each consensus
operation contains dozens to thousands of communication and
computing operations. As the scale of the system increases,
such algorithms that require a large number of iterations will
become increasingly inefﬁcient.
Moreover, some distributed methods based on reinforce-
ment learning (RL) have also been proposed to solve OP A
problems in real-time. In [13], a distributed Q-learning-based
algorithm is introduced to solve the OP A and unit commitment
problems. Dai et al. [14] present a distributed RL algorithm
for real-time OP A with unknown generation cost functions.
The work in [15] develops a consensus-based distributed RL
approach for OP A in MGs. In general, the above-mentioned
RL algorithms treat the input of an OP A problem (such as
a speciﬁc load) as a state and the corresponding optimal
solution as an action. Under this setting, an OP A problem is
transformed into a state-action pair. However, the state-action
pair is a discrete case, which means that the above-mentioned
RL algorithms are almost impossible to learn all feasible
state-action pairs representing t he whole relationship space of
an OP A problem. In other words, these RL algorithms lack
the necessary generalization capabilities so that they can only
respond to several trained cases in real-time, which is also
clearly shown in their case studies [13]–[15]. Therefore, when
a continuous time-varying load is taken into account, such
RL algorithms seem unable to solve the OP A problem in a
distributed framework in real-time.
Let us reconsider the OP A problem in a different way. It is,
in fact, a problem of trying to seek its optimal solution when
total load demand is given. From the system point of view,
an OP A optimization algorithm is indeed a system with the
input being the total load demand P
d and the output being the
optimal power generation from each dispatchable generator
(DG), i.e., P∗
i ,∀i , as illustrated in Fig. 1(a). All existing
algorithms are just doing one thing, that is to calculate P∗
i (out-
put) based on a given Pd (input) by using various numerical
approaches. Inspired by recent progress in machine learning
technologies [16]–[19], it is natural to ask the following ques-
tion: Can we treat the existing OPA optimization algorithm as
a “black box” and try to learn the relation between its input
and output? The answer should be positive. In fact, there are
some pioneering works employing artiﬁcial neural networks to
solve the OP A problem, which can be dated back to the 1990s,
see [20], [21]. However, due to the limited computational
resources at that time, only one hidden layer is considered in
those artiﬁcial neural networks, which inevitably degrades the
approximation accuracy. Also, we should mention some works
using DNN for real-time control of wireless resources [22]
and landings [23]–[25]. However, the above approaches are
all designed in a centralized way. As pointed out in [21], such
a centralized mechanism may su ffer from single-point failure
and inﬂexibility to MG system re-conﬁguration. Besides, its
individual computational cost during the training stage would
be very high when the system scales up.
To address these concerns, we propose a new distributed
learning-based optimization framework to solve the OP A
problem of an MG system in real time . The key idea
behind this approach is to treat the solution resulted from
a traditional OP A optimization algorithm as an unknown
nonlinear mapping from the input P
d to outputs P∗
i ,∀i =
1,..., N. Based on the properties of neural networks, this
mapping can be approximated by a deep neural network
(DNN), as shown in Fig. 1(b). As long as the constructed
neural network can accurately learn such nonlinear mapping,
then the OP A problem is solved. Besides, different from
the existing centralized network structure, a new distributed
learning-based optimization framework is proposed, where a
single large-scale DNN is decomposed into several small-scale
distributed DNNs. Each local DNN is only responsible to learn
the relationship between certain local information input and
local output P
∗
i . Intuitively, if such a DNN-based framework
can well approximate an OP A optimization algorithm, e.g.,
the approach in [1], then it would be quite computationally
cheap by simply passing the given load information to produce
the optimal power output P
∗
i . Compared to conventional
optimization algorithms, the proposed learning-based approach
only requires simple matrix-vector multiplication, which could
signiﬁcantly beneﬁt us in computational time saving and thus
is quite suitable for real-time OP A. In addition, it is worthy
to point out that training such a network is also fairly cheap
since the training samples can be easily obtained by running
the optimization algorithm to be learned.
The main contributions of this article can be summarized
as follows.
1) A new bio-inspired idea (from human thinking) for solv-
ing optimization problems is proposed. When human
beings explore unknown problems, ﬁrstly they usually
use their own “experience library” to form a rough judg-
ment, and then make precise decisions with meticulous
operations. Inspired by this scheme, similarly, the pro-
posed approach uses DNN as “experience library” to
quickly ﬁnd approximate solutions ﬁrstly, and then use
a speciﬁc algorithm to ﬁne-tune approximate solutions
to optimal solutions in a very short time.
2) Different from some existing work employing the DNN
technique for real-time optimization/control in other
areas in a centralized way, we ﬁrst propose distributed
DNNs to cooperatively solve an optimization problem in
a distributed manner.
3) The real-time distributed solution of the OP A problem is
given in this article, which, to the best of our knowledge,
has not been well solved by any existing studies.
4) The dynamic generator status is also well tackled by
our DNN-based approach, which is rarely considered

The rest of this article is organized as follows. Section II
mainly introduces the problem formulation. Before presenting
the main results in Section IV , some preliminary knowledge on
dynamic average consensus (DAC) algorithm, and a balance
generation and demand algorithm is reviewed in Section III.
Several experiment case studies are provided in Section V to
validate the effectiveness of the proposed approach. At last,
some concluding remarks are given in Section VI.
II. O
PTIMAL POWER ALLOCA TION IN MG S YSTEM
A. Problem F ormulation
OP A in MGs aims to allocate the power output among DGs
at lowest generation cost subject to the total load demand con-
straint and local generation constraints. It is usually formulated
as an optimization problem as follows [26] :

and wind turbines are usually treated as negative load and

B. Limitations of Conventional Numerical Optimization
Algorithms
In solving the OP A problem, the main concerns of existing
distributed numerical optimization algorithms, such as those
in [1], [26], [28], and [29], include high computational cost
and slow convergence rate. On the other hand, the intermittent
property of renewable energy sources in an MG system
results in rapid and unpredictable ﬂuctuations, which obvi-
ously demand a fast OP A algorithm to give real-time OP As
for such a system. Clear, it is very challenging for the existing
numerical optimization algorithms to meet the requirement.
To address such a challenging issue, we aim to re-solve the
OP A problem in a learning-based strategy.

IV . N EW DISTRIBUTED LEARNING BASED
OPTIMIZA TION APPROACH
In this section, to provide a distinguished real-time
OP A solution for islanded MG system, a new distributed
learning-based optimization approach is developed based on
previous reviewed techniques.
A. Bio-Inspired Algorithm Design
As illustrated in Fig. 3, when human beings explore
unknown problems, ﬁrstly they usually use their own “expe-
rience library” to form a rough judgment, and then make
precise decisions with meticulous operations. Inspired by
the above scheme, in this article, we propose a two-stage
DNN-based optimization algorithm. In the ﬁrst stage, the pro-
posed algorithm uses DNN that ac ting as “experience library”
to quickly ﬁnd an approximate solution, and then utilizes a
BGD algorithm to ﬁne-tune the approximate solution to the
optimal feasible solution in a very short time.
Fig. 4. Distributed learning based optimization approach for real-time OPA
in MG.
B. Algorithm Structure
The proposed algorithm structure is presented in Fig. 4,
which is designed with the aid of the two-layer multiagent
framework adopted from [31]. The entire algorithm is located
in the cyber layer, which is developed based on the idea of
“horizontal-distributed and verti cal-hierarchical.” Speciﬁcally,
as shown in Fig. 4, the whole algorithm is decomposed among
all the DGs, and each sub-algorithm consists of three cascad-
ing modules, i.e., DAC, DNN, and balance generation and
demand (BGD) algorithm. By allowing all the sub-algorithms
to communicate with their immediate neighbors, all the DGs in
the physical layer can cooperatively solve the OP A problem
formulated in (1). In practice, distributed communication in
MG systems can be applied to wireless networks, such as Zig-
Bee, WiFi, and cellular communication networks [32], [33].
The main procedure for each subalgorithm can be summa-
rized as the following three steps.
1) Step 1: Discover Global Load Demand by DAC: The
DAC module is designed in the ﬁrst layer of our framework,
as shown in Fig. 4. At each time instant t, every DAC module

Remark 2: The reason we select DAC rather than conven-
tional static average consensus algorithm is that DAC allows
a group of agents to track the average of their reference
time-varying inputs in a distributed manner [30], which per-
fectly meets our requirement for real-time capability.
Remark 3: It is worthy to emphasize again that even
though the problem (1) we formulate is a typical convex
optimization problem, under the distributed framework, almost
all existing distributed algorithms suffer from high compu-
tational and communication costs. The reason behind this is
that these distributed algorithms are designed in an iterative
way whereas each iteration requires at least one consensus
operation containing dozens to thousands of communication
and computing operations [1], [9]–[12]. As the scale of the
system increases, such algorith ms will become increasingly
inefﬁcient. In contrast, our DNN-based distributed algorithm
only requires three steps including two consensus operations
(DAC+ BGD) to obtain the optimal solution in a distributed
way. Therefore, from the perspective of algorithm design, our
proposed algorithm is considerably superior.
C. DNN Network Training
DNNs play the role of “experience library” in our frame-
work, thus one key step before algorithm implementation is to
train the local DNN networks off-line to let them well approx-
imate the nonlinear mapping relationship from (P
d(t)/N)
to P∗
i . In this subsection, a detailed DNN network training
procedure is provided, which includes data set generation,
training and validation, and testing stages.
1) Data Set Generation: In this stage, the training examples
are generated by running a tra ditional numerical optimiza-
tion algorithm, e.g., the hierar chical decentra lized optimiza-
tion (HDO) algorithm in [1] under different load demand
proﬁle Pd . The obtained optimal power output P∗

2) Training and V alidation Stage: We ﬁrst use the training

i

of the DNN. The optimization algorithm utilized for training
here is Adam, which is most commonly used in deep learning

performance, the weights are initialized by using the truncated

3) T esting Stage: Once the training stage is completed,
the DNN testing begins. The whole testing process for the
DNN network is quite simple. Firstly, distinct average load
demands (P
d/N) are fed into the well-trained DNN and collect
its outputs, i.e., P∗
i . Then we compare the outputs obtained by
the traditional HDO algorithm and the proposed DNN-based
method to evaluate the accuracy of our proposed DNN-based
architecture. MSE between the t esting data and network output
is used as an indicator to measure the network approxima-
tion accuracy. The smaller the MSE is, the more accurate
the approximation is. If MSE is larger than a pre-speciﬁed
threshold, we will return to the training stage and increase
the number of hidden layers and their corresponding neurons.
Besides, changing the activation function could also be an
alternative solution to impr ove the approximation accuracy.
Once the required accuracy is me t, we focus on the calculation
speed of the DNN-based framework to verify whether it is
capable of conducting real-time OP A.
D. Algorithm Implementation
The proposed distributed learning-based optimization algo-
rithm can be implemented and calculate the optimal power
output for each DG in real-time, once the off-line training of
the DNN network completes. To validate the effectiveness of
our proposed scheme, several case studies will be provided in
the next section.
Remark 4: The proposed distributed learning-based OP A
algorithm distinguishes from tra ditional numerical optimiza-
tion approaches in the following aspects: 1) no new mathe-
matical derivation of the optimization algorithm is required,
as we can use the well-established algorithm to generate the
training data set. Instead, we can immediately get P
∗
i by
feeding (Pd(t)/N) into the well-trained DNN network, where
just some simple matrix calculations are manipulated; 2) the
DNN-based method is a purely data-driven approach. If these
optimal power outputs and corresponding load demand data
are available, we even do not require to know the coefﬁcients
of cost functions in (1); and 3) the most signiﬁcant advantage
of the learning-based approach over traditional numerical opti-
mization algorithms is that it requires less time to obtain the
optimal solution online, which is quite suitable for real-time
optimization.
Remark 5: It is worth pointing out that there are several
other DNN architectures such as convolutional neural network
(CNN) [35], long short-term memory (LSTM) recurrent neural
network [36], autoencoder [37], and graph neural network
(GNN) [38]. These architectures have their own advantages
on feature extraction, classiﬁcation, and prediction. The reason
why we choose a fully connected DNN is that there lacks
a special structure of the f eatures of our formulated OP A

Therefore, considering that sophisticated feature extraction

E. Theoretical Analysis in DNN Approximation
It has been revealed in many existing works (see [18], [22],
[39], [40], [41]) that DNN can be utilized to approximate cer-
tain kinds of nonlinear functions and some “learnable” iterative
algorithms. However, it remains unclear whether the proposed
DNN can well approximate the existing OP A algorithms.
In addition, it is also unclear that the well-approximated DNN
is a ﬁnite-size network or not. In other words, at most how
many hidden layers and neurons are needed for such DNN to
approximate the OP A algorithm within given approximation
accuracy. In this subsection, based on the HDO algorithm
in [1], we try to theoretically analyze the DNN approximation
accuracy by giving quantitative numbers of the hidden layers
and their neurons, which is summarized in the following
Theorem.
Theorem 1: Consider a well-trained DNN with the structure
presented in Section IV -B, and the training strategy illustrated
in Section IV -C. It can well approximate Algorithm 1 (HDO
algorithm) with no errors by employing O(T) hidden layers
and O(NT ) neurons, where T is the iteration step needed for
HDO algorithm, and N is the total number of DGs.
Proof: See the Appendix.

VI. C
ONCLUSION
In this article, a new distributed learning-based real-time
optimization algorithm is proposed to allocate powers among
all the dispatchable DERs in an islanded MG system. Under
our proposed two-layer distributed framework, a DNN together
with DAC, and balance generation and demand techniques
are employed. Compared to traditional distributed numerical
optimization algorithms, the proposed learning-based approach
has the following advantages: 1) the optimal solution can be
directly obtained by simply feeding the load demand, which
takes much less computational time than traditional optimiza-
tion algorithm and thus can achieve real-time optimization;
2) different from conventional single DNN network, the pro-
posed distributed DNN structure is suitable for large-scale
system optimization; and 3) dynamic generator status is also
considered. The effectiveness of the proposed approach has
been validated by several case studies implemented on a 6-bus
islanded MG system and several large-scale MG systems.
It would be challenging but interesting to consider the
following topics as future research: 1) how to take the energy
storage system into account in the OP A problem formulation;
2) how to obtain the ground truth of a non-convex OP A
problem; and 3) integration of renewable energy prediction
with our proposed DNN based framework.
